title: Problem Overview: Distance Multiplicities
content:
**Erdős Problem #94** ($44 prize): given n points in convex position in ℝ², let f(u) count how many pairs of points are at distance u. The trivial identity ∑ f(u) = C(n,2) means the multiplicities partition all pairs. The question: how large can ∑ f(u)² be?

**Fishburn** proved ∑ f(u)² = O(n³). **Lefmann-Theile (1995)** extended to the weaker 'no three collinear' condition. The **regular n-gon** achieves Θ(n³), making the bound tight. The **Erdős-Fishburn conjecture** (open) predicts the regular n-gon is the unique maximizer.

**Why it matters**: The bound constrains how concentrated the distance distribution can be in a convex polygon — a central question in discrete geometry.
mathContext: Imports: PiL2 for the Euclidean plane ℝ² as EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2), Convex.Hull for convex position, Finset.Basic for the combinatorial infrastructure.

title: Point and PointConfig
content:
**Point** is the Euclidean plane ℝ², represented as `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)` — the product space with the L² norm. **PointConfig** is a finite set of points (`Finset Point`). Using a `Finset` ensures cardinality is well-defined and summations are computable.

**distanceSet** computes all positive pairwise distances: it takes all pairs `(p, q) ∈ P × P` via `P ×ˢ P`, maps to their distance, and filters out 0 (the self-distance). The result is the set d(P) = {dist(p,q) : p, q ∈ P, p ≠ q}.
mathContext: EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2) = PiLp 2 (fun _ : Fin 2 => ℝ). `P ×ˢ P` is Finset.product P P in Mathlib 4. The filter `· > 0` removes self-distances.

title: Distance Multiplicity and Sum of Squares
content:
**distanceMultiplicity P u**: counts ordered pairs (p, q) with p ≠ q and dist(p,q) = u. Each unordered pair {p,q} contributes 2 (once as (p,q) and once as (q,p)).

**unorderedMultiplicity P u**: divides by 2, giving the standard f(u) that counts unordered pairs.

**sumSquaredMultiplicities P**: ∑_{u ∈ d(P)} f̃(u)², the central quantity.

**countEqualDistancePairs P**: counts quadruples (p,q,r,s) with p≠q, r≠s, and d(p,q) = d(r,s). This equals 4 ∑ f(u)² — a useful reformulation for incidence-based proofs.
mathContext: `Finset.filter` on `P ×ˢ P` selects pairs at a given distance. The quadruple count uses `(P ×ˢ P) ×ˢ (P ×ˢ P)` with pattern-matched anonymous constructors.

title: Convex Position and No-Three-Collinear
content:
**InConvexPosition P**: no point lies in the convex hull of the remaining points. This captures 'vertices of a convex polygon' — removing any point strictly reduces the convex hull.

**NoThreeCollinear P**: no three points p, q, r ∈ P are collinear (lie on a common line). This is **strictly weaker** than convex position. The Lefmann-Theile theorem improves Fishburn's by working under this weaker hypothesis.

**convex_implies_no_collinear** (axiom): InConvexPosition → NoThreeCollinear.
mathContext: `convexHull ℝ (↑(P.erase p) : Set Point)` — convex hull of P with p removed. `Collinear ℝ S` means S is contained in an affine line.

title: Baseline Identity: ∑ f(u) = C(n, 2)
content:
**sum_multiplicities** (axiom): ∑_{u ∈ d(P)} f̃(u) = C(|P|, 2).

The multiplicities f(u) partition all C(n,2) unordered pairs by their distance. While trivial conceptually, the Lean proof requires showing each unordered pair contributes exactly once, that f(u) is always even (pairs come with their reversal), and that Nat.choose n 2 = n*(n-1)/2.

In the predecessor stub, Aristotle proved this fully via Finset.sum_image' and an involution argument. It is axiomatized here for brevity.
mathContext: Nat.choose n 2 in Mathlib. The evenness of distanceMultiplicity uses the involution (p,q) ↦ (q,p), which pairs up all ordered pairs at each distance.

title: Fishburn's Theorem and Lefmann-Theile
content:
**fishburn_theorem** (axiom): For any convex polygon configuration P, ∑ f(u)² ≤ C·n³ for some absolute constant C > 0.

The proof idea: reformulate as counting quadruples (p,q,r,s) with d(p,q) = d(r,s). In a convex polygon, two distinct chords of equal length are 'parallel' in a precise sense. Counting valid quadruples combinatorially yields O(n³).

**lefmann_theile_theorem** (axiom): The same O(n³) bound holds under NoThreeCollinear alone. The proof uses a more sophisticated incidence argument, avoiding the special structure of convex polygons.
mathContext: Both axioms: ∃ C : ℝ, C > 0 ∧ ∀ P, [condition P] → sumSquaredMultiplicities P ≤ C * P.card ^ 3. The Lefmann-Theile extension is related to Szemerédi-Trotter-type incidence bounds.

title: Regular n-gon: Matching the Upper Bound
content:
The **regular n-gon** is axiomatized with three key properties: (1) exactly n points, (2) convex position, (3) Θ(n³) bounds on ∑ f(u)².

Why Θ(n³)? The regular n-gon has ⌊n/2⌋ distinct distances. Each distance 2sin(kπ/n) (for k = 1,...,⌊n/2⌋) has multiplicity n — every vertex has exactly one neighbor at each distance. So ∑ f(u)² ≈ ⌊n/2⌋ · n² = Θ(n³). This matches Fishburn's upper bound.

The construction via cos/sin on the unit circle is axiomatized rather than constructed directly, avoiding type-coercion complexity with EuclideanSpace.
mathContext: The regular n-gon construction: {(cos(2πk/n), sin(2πk/n)) : k = 0,...,n-1}. In EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2), this requires coercing Finset.range n from ℕ to ℝ for the cos/sin arguments.

title: Erdős-Fishburn Conjecture
content:
**ErdosFishburnConjecture** (open): For all sufficiently large n and any convex n-gon configuration P, ∑ f(u)² ≤ ∑ f_reg(u)². The regular polygon is the unique maximizer.

Computational evidence: verified for n ≤ 10 (OEIS A387858).

**SumSquaredThetaN3**: Records the Θ(n³) fact as a Prop, combining fishburn_theorem (upper bound) and regularNGon_cubic (lower bound). Together these axioms establish that ∑ f(u)² = Θ(n³) for convex n-gons — the main result of the problem.
mathContext: `sumSquaredMultiplicities (regularNGon n)` uses the axiomatized regularNGon function. The Θ(n³) Prop is derivable from the existing axioms without additional sorry.
